passages.happening:
As Jesus walks along, he sees a man who has been blind from birth (verse 1). His disciples ask a question many people asked then: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” (verse 2).

Jesus answers, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him” (verse 3). Then he adds, “While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work” (verse 4), and, “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (verse 5).

Then he acts. He spits on the ground, makes some mud, and puts it on the man's eyes. He tells him, “Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam” (verse 7). John adds that Siloam means ‘Sent’. The man goes, washes, and comes back seeing.
passages.hearers:
The disciples' question shows a belief that was common in the ancient world, and is still common today: if something is wrong with you, someone must have done something wrong. The disciples are not sure who. If the man was born blind, either his parents had sinned, or somehow he had sinned before he was born. Later Jewish teachers argued about it too. The Babylonian Talmud, written down centuries after Jesus, records one rabbi teaching that there is no suffering without sin, and then records the rabbis disproving him. The book of Job had already fought this battle. Job's friends insisted he must have sinned, and at the end God rebukes them for what they said (Job 42:7).

A man blind from birth had almost no way to earn a living. He sat and begged, and people knew him as ‘the man who used to sit and beg’ (verse 8). The disciples talk about him, perhaps in his hearing, as a case to discuss. Jesus stops and deals with him as a person.

Spit was widely thought to have healing power. The Roman historian Tacitus tells how, around AD 70, a blind man in Alexandria begged the emperor Vespasian to touch his eyes with spittle. Jesus uses ordinary things, earth and spit and water, and a long walk. Some readers have also noticed that God first formed man from the dust of the ground. Here Jesus takes the ground and finishes what was missing.

The Pool of Siloam lay at the south end of Jerusalem. A large stepped pool from this period was found there in 2004, and many take it to be the pool of this story. John notes that its name means ‘Sent’, and Jesus is the one the Father sent.
passages.ot: The Law spoke of God “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me” (Exodus 20:5). But the prophets also said, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son” (Ezekiel 18:20). The Law protected blind people: “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14). And the Scriptures looked for a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened” (Isaiah 35:5), because “the LORD opens the eyes of the blind” (Psalm 146:8). In the beginning “the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground” (Genesis 2:7).
passages.hard:
Verse 3 needs to be read carefully, because it has been used to hurt people. First, what Jesus clearly says: neither the man nor his parents sinned. His blindness was not a punishment. Disability is not punishment for sin, the person's own or anyone else's. Jesus says so plainly, and these notes say so plainly.

Second, what about ‘this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him’? Does it mean God made a man blind for decades just to have something to fix? Christians read it in more than one way. Many read it as Jesus turning the question around. The disciples asked who was to blame. Jesus says the right question is what God will do here, now. The verse speaks of God's purpose reaching into the man's life, without saying God sent the blindness as a show.

Some scholars point out that the oldest copies of John have no punctuation. They propose a full stop after ‘Neither this man nor his parents sinned’. Then the next words join verse 4: so that the works of God may be shown in him, we must work while it is day. On this reading Jesus does not explain why the man was born blind at all. He says what he is going to do about it. Most Bibles keep the usual punctuation. It is a view worth knowing, and it is offered here as a view.

All these readings agree on what matters most. Jesus refuses to treat a man's body as a puzzle about guilt, and he answers suffering by acting.
passages.asks:
If you live with a disability, or love someone who does, hear this clearly: it is not a punishment, and you are not a riddle for other people to solve. Jesus would not let his friends discuss the man as a case. He stopped, he touched him, and he spoke to him.

And the man is not just a lesson in this chapter. He is its hero. Watch him in the scenes that follow: he speaks for himself, he answers powerful men with courage and humor, and he is the one who ends up seeing most clearly of all.

passages.happening:
The neighbors can hardly believe it. “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?” they ask (verse 8). Some say it is. Others say, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man keeps saying, “I am the one” (verse 9).

They ask how his eyes were opened. He tells them simply: “The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight” (verse 11). Where is Jesus now? “I do not know,” he says (verse 12).

They bring him to the Pharisees. John now tells us that the healing happened on a Sabbath (verse 14). The man tells his story again, more briefly: “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see” (verse 15). The Pharisees split. Some say, “This man is not from God, for He does not keep the Sabbath.” Others ask, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” (verse 16). So they ask the man what he thinks, and he answers, “He is a prophet” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
For years the neighbors had seen only a beggar. Now that he can see, some of them are not sure he is the same man. When people have known you only by your need, it can be hard for them to see you any other way.

‘I am the one’ is the same Greek pair of words, egō eimi, that Jesus used in chapter 8. On the man's lips it simply means ‘It's me’. He is claiming his own name and story.

Why does the Sabbath matter so much? The Law said no work on the Sabbath, and teachers worked out what counted as work. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, and kneading is one of them. Making mud with spit and earth could be counted as kneading. Healing was a harder question still. A long blindness was not a danger to life, so the healing could have waited a day. Jesus did not wait. As in chapter 5, he heals on the Sabbath anyway.

Notice that the Pharisees are divided. Some think a man who breaks the Sabbath cannot be from God. Others think a sinner could not do signs like this. Both groups are Jews, and both are trying to be faithful to the Law. The question is a real one, and John lets it stand for a moment before the story moves on.
passages.ot: The Sabbath command was clear: “Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:9-10). The Pharisees took it seriously. Moses had also promised that God would raise up a prophet: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:18). When the man says, ‘He is a prophet’, he uses the highest title he knows so far.
passages.asks: The man does not know much yet. He does not know where Jesus is. He does not know what to call him beyond ‘the man they call Jesus’ and then ‘a prophet’. But he tells the truth about what happened to him, again and again. Faith often grows like this: not from having every answer, but from refusing to deny what you know has happened.

passages.happening:
The authorities do not believe the man had really been blind until they call his parents (verse 18). “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is it that he can now see?” they ask (verse 19).

The parents answer carefully. “We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind. But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself” (verses 20-21).

John explains why: “His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews. For the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
‘Afraid of the Jews’ cannot mean afraid of the Jewish people. The parents are Jews themselves, and so are their son, the neighbors, and the Pharisees. Here the phrase means the authorities, the leaders who had the power to put people out. John's book page explains how the phrase is used.

To be put out of the synagogue was a heavy thing. The synagogue was the center of a town's life: its prayer, its reading of Scripture, its friendships and its help in hard times. To lose it was to lose your place among your own people. No wonder the parents step back. They do not deny their son, but they will not stand next to him either.
passages.ot: Being cut off from the assembly was an old threat in Israel. In Ezra's day anyone who did not come when called would be “expelled from the assembly of the exiles” (Ezra 10:8). The Psalms hold out comfort for those left alone: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).
passages.hard: What do historians say about this? Many scholars think John's book was finished in a time of painful separation, when some Jews who believed in Jesus had been put out of their synagogues (see also 12:42 and 16:2). In 1968 J. Louis Martyn linked this verse to a synagogue prayer against heretics from late in the first century, and argued that John was telling his own community's story through Jesus' story. Many scholars now doubt that link. Others argue that local exclusions like this could well have happened in Jesus' own lifetime. Either way, the chapter describes what particular leaders decided, not the character of a people. The verse has been used to stir hatred of Jews, and it gives no ground for that.
passages.asks:
It is easy to judge the parents. But fear for your place, your income, your family's standing, is real. Many people have stayed quiet when they should have spoken, because the cost of speaking felt too high. If that is you, the story does not shame you. It shows you a son who spoke anyway, and a Lord who went looking for him.

If you have been pushed out of a church or a community for telling the truth, you are in this chapter too. Keep reading. The man who was put out is the one Jesus goes to find.

passages.t: I was blind, but now I see
passages.happening:
The leaders call the man back a second time. “Give glory to God!” they say. “We know that this man is a sinner” (verse 24). The man answers, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” (verse 25).

They ask again how it happened. Now the man loses patience: “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?” (verse 27). They insult him: “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (verse 28). They know God spoke to Moses, but they do not know where this man is from (verse 29).

“That is remarkable indeed!” the man says. “You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes” (verse 30). He reasons that God listens to those who worship him and do his will, and that no one has ever heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind. “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing” (verse 33). They reply, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they throw him out (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
‘Give glory to God’ was a solemn formula. It was what Joshua said to Achan when he wanted him to confess the truth. The leaders mean: ‘Stop protecting this man, and tell us the truth.’ They have already decided what the truth is.

The man will not be moved. He will not say what he does not know. He will not deny what he does know. His one sentence, ‘I was blind, but now I see’, has become one of the best-known sentences in the Bible. John Newton's hymn Amazing Grace, written most likely for a New Year's Day service in 1773 and printed in 1779, echoes it: ‘was blind, but now I see’.

He also has a sharp wit. ‘Do you also want to become His disciples?’ is a joke at their expense, and they know it. A beggar who had never had a voice is now arguing with the teachers of the Law, and winning.

‘We know that God does not listen to sinners’ (verse 31) is the man's argument, not a rule Jesus gives. He means that God does not stand behind people who defy him. The Scriptures say something like it, but they also show God hearing sinners who cry to him for mercy, as he heard King Manasseh (2 Chronicles 33:13).

‘You were born in utter sin’ shows that the leaders hold the same belief the disciples did at the start: his blindness proved his sin. They had refused to believe he was born blind. Now they use his blindness against him.
passages.ot: The leaders use Joshua's words to Achan: “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and make a confession to Him” (Joshua 7:19). The man's reasoning echoes the Psalms, “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18), and the Proverbs, “The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous” (Proverbs 15:29). Isaiah had promised that one day “out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see” (Isaiah 29:18).
passages.asks: You do not need every answer to tell the truth about what God has done in your life. The man could not explain Jesus. He could only say, ‘I was blind, but now I see.’ That was enough to stand on, even when powerful people mocked him for it. If you are unsure about many things, start with the one thing you know.

passages.happening:
Jesus hears that they have thrown the man out, and he goes and finds him. “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” he asks (verse 35). “Who is He, Sir?” the man replies. “Tell me so that I may believe in Him” (verse 36). “You have already seen Him,” Jesus says. “He is the One speaking with you” (verse 37). The man says, “Lord, I believe,” and he worships Jesus (verse 38).

Then Jesus says, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind” (verse 39). Some Pharisees nearby ask, “Are we blind too?” (verse 40). “If you were blind,” Jesus answers, “you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
The man was put out, and then he was found. Nobody else in the story goes looking for him. Jesus does.

‘The Son of Man’ is the name Jesus most often uses for himself. It comes from Daniel's vision of one ‘like the Son of Man’ who receives a kingdom from God. The man does not know the title, but he is ready to believe. And ‘You have already seen Him’ has a wonderful double sense. For the first time in his life, he has seen anyone at all, and the one he is looking at is the Son of Man.

Notice how his words about Jesus grow through the chapter: ‘the man they call Jesus’ (verse 11), ‘a prophet’ (verse 17), ‘from God’ (verse 33), and now ‘Lord’, as he worships him (verse 38). As his eyes are opened, so is his faith.

The leaders go the other way. They start sure of what they know and end unable to see what is in front of them. That is the ‘judgment’ Jesus speaks of. It is not a sentence handed down from outside. It is what happens when light comes: some people walk toward it, and some shut their eyes. Jesus' words are aimed at those who are certain they already see. The man who knew he was blind was healed. The men who were sure they could see stayed where they were.
passages.ot: Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13). Isaiah was told about a people who would be “ever seeing, but never perceiving” (Isaiah 6:9). Jesus' words in verse 39 take up that warning, and also Isaiah's promise that God would come “to open the eyes of the blind” (Isaiah 42:7).
passages.hard:
Is Jesus saying that people who know they are blind are free of sin? Not quite. He is using blindness in two ways. To be blind and know it, and so to ask for help, is the beginning of healing. To be blind and insist you can see is the condition that keeps a person from help. ‘Your guilt remains’ is said to those who claim to see and refuse the light in front of them.

This warning is not about one group long ago. It reaches every reader who is sure of being right, religious readers most of all. The people in this chapter who saw least were the ones most confident in their own knowledge of God. Christians have often stood in that place too, and the warning reaches them first.
passages.asks: The chapter began with a question about who was to blame. It ends with a question each reader has to answer: ‘Are we blind too?’ The safest place to stand is where the man stood, knowing that you need your eyes opened, and ready to believe when the light comes. If you have been put out, by a church or a family or a town, remember that Jesus went looking for the man they threw out.
